stem: The marks scored by 7 students in a test are: 15, 22, 8, 31, 18, 27, 11. What is the median mark?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Sorting the 7 values gives 8, 11, 15, 18, 22, 27, 31. The middle (4th) value is 18.
22 is the value at position 5 in the sorted list; picking it confuses the median position with one position further right.
19 is the arithmetic mean (132/7 = 18.86 rounded to 19), so the student used the average instead of locating the sorted middle.
15 is the 3rd value in the sorted list; a slip in computing the middle position as 3 instead of 4 (i.e., applying (7-1)/2 = 3 rather than (7+1)/2 = 4) gives this.

explanation: Sort the 7 observations in ascending order: 8, 11, 15, 18, 22, 27, 31. For n = 7 (odd), the median is the ((7+1)/2) = 4th value, which is 18.

explanation_sections.punchline: For an odd number of observations the median is the exact middle value of the sorted list.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: raw unsorted data, odd n. Sort the data, locate position (n+1)/2 = 4, read off the value directly.
explanation_sections.lesson: Always sort first; median is a position, not a formula applied to the original order.
explanation_sections.timing: 45 s. Sort mentally in two passes. The trap is reading off the wrong position or computing the mean instead.
